strengths: Identifies a clear and important limitation of group DRO when applied to CTC-based multilingual ASR: length-dependent scaling of CTC loss creates spurious differences between group losses, causing group DRO to overweight groups that are not actually the worst-performing.

Proposes two complementary, well-motivated fixes (length-matched batching and a smoothed maximization objective) and provides a clean theoretical derivation showing the new objective generalizes group DRO (recovering it as α→∞) via a Lagrangian analysis.

Thorough empirical evaluation across five distinct language sets, two pretrained backbones (XLS-R, MMS), and both balanced and unbalanced training data conditions, consistently showing improvements in worst-language CER and average CER over both baseline and group DRO.
Solid ablation study isolating the contribution of each proposed component, showing both are necessary and that the smoothing term has the largest effect.
Insightful qualitative analysis of group weight trajectories (Figure 2) that visually demonstrates the instability of group DRO versus the stability of CTC-DRO during training.
Practical significance: minimal added computational cost, applicability to an important real-world problem (multilingual ASR equity), and promise of public code/models supports reproducibility.
Good related-work grounding, including explicit acknowledgment of a prior negative result (Gao et al., 2022) for DRO in ASR, positioning the contribution clearly.
weaknesses: Experimental scale is fairly limited: only five language sets of six languages each, with just one hour of training data per language in the primary setting, which may limit generalizability of the findings to larger-scale multilingual ASR systems.

No comparison to other robustness/calibration baselines beyond vanilla group DRO (e.g., loss calibration methods from Oren et al. 2019 or Słowik & Bottou 2022, or simple heuristics like per-utterance length normalization or group upsampling), making it hard to judge how much of the gain is attributable to the specific smoothing design versus simpler fixes.

Results appear to be based on single training runs per configuration; no reported variance across seeds or statistical significance testing, which is concerning given the paper's own observation that group weight dynamics (and by extension final performance) can fluctuate substantially during training.

Checkpoint selection for CTC-DRO/group DRO models is based on best worst-language CER improvement on the dev set, which is a fairly specific selection criterion that could favor the proposed method over the baseline in ways not fully controlled for.
Hyperparameter search for α is limited to three values {0.1, 0.5, 1}, with little discussion of sensitivity or guidance for practitioners on how to select it in new settings.
Claims of broader applicability to other domains (e.g., language modeling, video transcription) in the conclusion are speculative and untested within the paper.

The connection between the smoothing hyperparameter α and the underlying goal of correcting for irreducible loss differences across groups is argued qualitatively/theoretically but not empirically validated against ground-truth irreducible loss estimates.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: convincingly demonstrates (both theoretically and empirically) that CTC loss magnitudes are not directly comparable across groups due to length/linguistic/acoustic differences, undermining standard group DRO.

The proposed smoothed maximization objective is theoretically grounded, with a clean derivation (via the Hedge algorithm and Lagrangian analysis) showing it generalizes group DRO and reduces to it as alpha to infinity.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across 5 randomly selected language sets, 2 pretrained backbones (XLS-R, MMS), and both balanced/unbalanced data regimes, with consistent gains over both baseline and vanilla group DRO.
Useful ablation study isolating the contributions of length-matched batching and the smoothed objective, showing both components matter and that the smoothing term is especially critical.
Group weight trajectory analysis (Figure 2) provides intuitive, convincing evidence for why CTC-DRO stabilizes training relative to group DRO.
Method is computationally cheap (only a scalar weight per group), making it practically easy to adopt.
weaknesses: Experimental scale is quite limited: only six languages per set and just one hour of training data per language in the main (balanced) setting; unclear whether findings hold at the scale of real multilingual ASR systems (in the hundreds of languages, as in the underlying MMS model), despite the paper's motivation being large-scale multilingual accessibility.
Unbalanced/more-data experiments are only run for 2 of the 5 language sets, leaving open questions about consistency of gains with more realistic (non-uniform) training data amounts.

The group DRO baseline performs surprisingly poorly, often increasing average CER and LID accuracy substantially (e.g., dropping LID accuracy from ~97% to ~63-67% in several settings) — this looks like a very weak baseline and raises the question whether group DRO was adequately tuned; no discussion of why group DRO collapses so severely or whether additional regularization (as in Sagawa et al. 2020) was tried.

Hyperparameter search space for both group DRO and CTC-DRO is narrow (2 values for step size, 3 for alpha), which may not give group DRO or ablated variants a fair chance and raises concerns about the robustness of comparisons.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting; all results appear to be single runs, making it hard to assess whether improvements are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially given the relatively small test sets (10 minutes per language).

The model selection procedure (choosing the checkpoint with the largest CER improvement on worst-performing language on the dev set) is somewhat favorable to the proposed method and not clearly matched for the baseline, raising fairness-of-comparison concerns.

No direct empirical comparison to alternative solutions to the DRO-loss-miscalibration problem mentioned in related work (Oren et al. 2019; Słowik & Bottou 2022), only a qualitative dismissal on computational-cost grounds.
Despite claimed broader applicability to other variable-length-sequence domains (language modeling, video transcription), no experiments outside ASR/CTC are provided, making these claims speculative.

Absolute performance remains poor in several settings even with CTC-DRO (e.g., worst-language CER of 77.1% for XLS-R on set 5), which somewhat tempers the practical significance of the reported relative improvements.

The theoretical justification for the specific choice of log(q+alpha) smoothing (versus other possible smoothing schemes) is not well motivated beyond convenience of recovering group DRO as a special case.

strengths: Clearly motivated and well-diagnosed problem: the paper carefully explains why CTC loss scaling with sequence length breaks the group-comparability assumption underlying group DRO, supported by a concrete empirical illustration (Figure 1, Spanish example).

Principled algorithmic contribution: the smoothed maximization objective is derived as a genuine generalization of the group DRO objective (provably reduces to group DRO as α→∞), with a clean theoretical analysis (Lagrangian derivation) showing the optimal weight retains the desired loss-proportional property while being smoothed.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 randomly selected language sets, 2 pretrained backbones (XLS-R, MMS), and both balanced and unbalanced training data regimes, showing consistent improvements over baseline and group DRO in worst-case and average CER.
Thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of length-matched batching and the smoothed objective, showing both are necessary and that the smoothing objective is the primary driver.
Insightful analysis of group weight trajectories during training (Figure 2), providing intuitive evidence for why CTC-DRO stabilizes training relative to group DRO's degenerate weight collapse.
Practically relevant: the method has minimal computational overhead (only a scalar weight per group) and is straightforward to integrate into existing CTC-based multilingual ASR pipelines.
Honest positioning relative to prior negative results (Gao et al., 2022) on DRO for ASR, and clear articulation of why naive length normalization alone is insufficient.
Promise of public code and model release aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to relatively small language sets (6 languages, mostly 1 hour of training data per language-corpus pair); it remains unclear how well the method scales to settings with many more languages or larger, more heterogeneous training sets.

The only robust-optimization baseline is vanilla group DRO; other loss-calibration or rebalancing approaches discussed in Section 2.3 (e.g., Oren et al., Słowik & Bottou) are dismissed as impractical but not empirically compared, even in a simplified form.

Model/checkpoint selection for CTC-DRO and group DRO is based on the largest worst-language CER improvement on the dev set, which could bias reported results somewhat favorably toward the paper's own metric of interest.

The detailed ablation (Section 6.1) and group-weight analysis (Section 6.2) are conducted on only one language set (set 5) and one backbone (XLS-R for the weight analysis), so it is unclear whether these qualitative findings generalize to the other four sets.
No variance/robustness analysis across multiple training seeds is reported, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of the (sometimes modest) CER differences.

The choice of the specific smoothing function log(q+α) is motivated primarily by its convenient limiting behavior and empirical success rather than a deeper theoretical argument for why this particular form is optimal among possible smoothing choices.
Claims about broader applicability to other variable-length-sequence domains (language modeling, video transcription) are speculative and not empirically supported within the paper.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated identification of a specific failure mode of group DRO when applied with the CTC loss (scaling with input/output length, irreducible loss differences across languages), supported by both intuitive explanation and a formal derivation (Section 2.3).

The proposed CTC-DRO algorithm combines two complementary, well-justified fixes (length-matched batching and a smoothed group-weight update), and the paper provides a clean derivation showing the smoothed objective is a principled generalization of group DRO that reduces to the original as alpha grows.

Extensive and carefully designed experiments: 5 diverse language sets from ML-SUPERB 2.0, two backbone models (MMS, XLS-R), balanced and unbalanced data regimes, consistently showing CTC-DRO reduces worst-language CER (up to 47.1%) and average CER (up to 32.9%) relative to both baseline and group DRO.

Thorough robustness and ablation studies: subtractive ablation isolating the contribution of each component, multi-seed experiments confirming stability of gains, sensitivity analysis on the batch-duration hyperparameter, alternative normalization baselines (frame/target length normalization) showing naive fixes are insufficient, and a scalability experiment to 18 languages.
Useful qualitative analysis of group weight dynamics over training (Figure 2 and appendix figures) that intuitively explains why CTC-DRO is more stable than group DRO.

Good transparency about limitations (e.g., WER vs CER discrepancies, best-language performance analysis with statistical significance tests), and a clear reproducibility statement with dataset/hyperparameter details in the appendix.

Practical significance: the method adds minimal computational overhead (comparable wall-clock training time to baseline) while addressing a real-world problem (cross-lingual disparities in ASR) relevant to accessibility.
weaknesses: Group sizes in main experiments are small (6 languages, ~1 hour of data each); while a scalability experiment to 18 languages is included, its gains are noticeably smaller (8-9% vs up to 47%) and the hyperparameter search for that setting appears less rigorous (single run, no stated multi-seed validation), raising questions about how well the method scales to realistic multilingual ASR settings (hundreds of languages, larger datasets).

Results are somewhat inconsistent for the average CER/WER metric: e.g., XLS-R on set 3 shows slightly worse average CER than baseline, and the WER analysis in Appendix F.2 shows XLS-R's average WER increasing marginally despite CER improving, complicating the overall narrative of consistent gains.

The group DRO baseline performs very poorly and often worse than the plain baseline (e.g., increasing average CER in all 14 settings), which, while explained theoretically, makes the comparison feel somewhat like a strawman; a broader set of baselines/alternative DRO variants (beyond citing why they are unsuitable) would strengthen the empirical claims.

The theoretical derivation shows that the smoothed objective still increases weight monotonically with loss (Eq. 17), but does not provide a rigorous theoretical justification connecting the smoothing hyperparameter alpha to the actual irreducible-loss/length-bias problem it is meant to solve; the choice of alpha remains an empirically tuned hyperparameter without principled selection guidance.
The claimed broader applicability to other domains (e.g., text classification, video transcription, medical applications) is speculative and not empirically validated in the paper.

The selection of language sets, while stratified by CER percentiles, is still relatively small-scale and somewhat curated, which may limit the generality of the conclusions to the full diversity of low-resource multilingual ASR conditions.

strengths: Clearly identifies and formally analyzes a real problem: CTC loss magnitudes are not comparable across language groups due to length and acoustic/linguistic differences, which breaks the assumptions underlying group DRO.
The proposed smoothed maximization objective is theoretically grounded via a Lagrangian analysis showing it recovers group DRO as a limiting case while still preserving loss-monotonic weighting.

Extensive empirical evaluation: five diverse language sets from ML-SUPERB 2.0, balanced and unbalanced data regimes, two backbone models (XLS-R, MMS), an ablation isolating the two proposed components, multi-seed robustness checks, group-weight trajectory visualizations, a scalability experiment to 18 languages, and normalization ablations in the appendix.

Results consistently show group DRO can catastrophically fail (large worst-language CER increases, degenerate weight collapse) while CTC-DRO stabilizes weights and improves worst-language CER in all tested sets.
Good reproducibility documentation (hyperparameter grids, dataset composition tables, training time reporting) and promise to release code/models.
weaknesses: Training/dev/test sets are extremely small (1 hour train, 10 min dev/test per language), and hyperparameters (ηq, α) are selected on this tiny dev set per language set, raising concerns about overfitting hyperparameter choices to noise rather than a generalizable method.

Multi-seed robustness results (Appendix F.4) are mixed: for XLS-R on set 3, CTC-DRO's mean worst-language CER is actually slightly worse than baseline (avg delta -1.5, only 2/4 seeds favor CTC-DRO), undercutting the claim that gains are stable/robust.

Average CER improvements are inconsistent across settings (e.g., XLS-R on balanced set 3 is worse with CTC-DRO; MMS average CER is slightly worse than baseline in the 18-language scaling experiment), so the paper's headline aggregate improvement numbers (up to 47.1%/32.9%) reflect best cases rather than a uniformly reliable improvement.

The group DRO baseline appears comparatively under-explored relative to CTC-DRO: it is unclear whether the same breadth of hyperparameter search (α equivalent, batch sampling variants) was applied to it, making the large reported gap partly an artifact of asymmetric tuning effort.

The 'Comparison with other approaches' section dismisses several relevant alternatives (Oren et al. 2019, Słowik & Bottou 2022, Lokhande et al. 2022, RL-based methods) using qualitative/computational-cost arguments rather than actual empirical baselines, weakening the claim of the method's relative superiority.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core algorithmic change is an α-regularized (damped) multiplicative-weights update, a fairly standard smoothing/regularization trick, combined with straightforward length-matched batch sampling; neither component is conceptually new to the robust-optimization or ASR literature.

The worst-performing language identity shifts between baseline and CTC-DRO in several settings, and in some cases the model only redistributes errors among languages (e.g., Korean improves while Khmer remains the new worst) rather than uniformly reducing disparity, which is not deeply analyzed for its implications on fairness.

Statistical testing for best-language degradation (Appendix F.5) uses very small sample sizes (paired t-tests over ~7-10 configurations), which limits the reliability of claims of 'no significant degradation.'
Broader claims of applicability to other domains and modalities (medical, text classification, video transcription) are speculative and untested within the paper.

strengths: Clear identification and theoretical analysis of a real, practically important failure mode of group DRO when applied to CTC losses, motivated by concrete observations (e.g., length distribution differences across languages causing spurious loss disparities).

The proposed method (length-matched batching + smoothed maximization objective) is well-motivated, simple, and theoretically grounded, including a derivation showing the smoothed objective is a principled generalization of group DRO that recovers group DRO as a special case (alpha to infinity).

Extensive empirical evaluation across five diverse language sets from ML-SUPERB 2.0, two model backbones (XLS-R, MMS), balanced and unbalanced data settings, with consistent and substantial improvements in worst-language CER (up to 47.1%) and average CER (up to 32.9%).

Thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of each component (length-matched losses and smoothed objective), showing both are necessary and that removing either significantly hurts performance.

Good supplementary analyses: group weight dynamics over training (showing CTC-DRO produces much more stable weights than group DRO), robustness to random seeds, sensitivity to batch duration hyperparameter, normalization-only baselines showing simple fixes are insufficient, best-language performance analysis (no significant degradation), WER evaluation for a subset, and a scalability experiment to 18 languages.

Practical relevance: the method has minimal computational overhead (only a single scalar per group), is compatible with existing CTC-based multilingual ASR pipelines, and the paper commits to releasing code and models.

Honest discussion of limitations (disparities reduced but not eliminated) and clear positioning relative to alternative approaches (calibration, RL-based methods) with justification for why these are not suitable here.
weaknesses: The number of groups per experiment (six) is relatively small, and although a scalability experiment with 18 languages is included, the hyperparameter search there was less exhaustive (single run per setting) and gains are more modest, leaving some uncertainty about behavior at the scale of hundreds of languages typical of real multilingual ASR systems.

Hyperparameters (eta_q, alpha) are tuned per language set on the development set, and there is no discussion of how sensitive real-world deployment would be to needing this per-setting tuning when the group structure or number of groups changes.

The improvement is not universal: group DRO is a fairly weak baseline in this setting (it degrades average CER in every configuration), so the comparison mostly demonstrates that CTC-DRO fixes group DRO's known failure mode rather than beating a strong diverse set of alternative robustness/fairness methods for ASR head-to-head empirically (the comparison with other methods in Section 7 is qualitative/argued rather than empirical).

Training data per language is quite small (~1 hour), which is realistic for low-resource ASR but leaves open questions about how results generalize to larger-scale, more standard multilingual ASR training regimes.

The selection of 'worst-performing language' checkpoint based on development set worst-language CER could be seen as a form of tuning specifically to the reported metric, which may somewhat inflate the highlighted improvements relative to a fixed-checkpoint selection protocol.
